sections.title: The AI landlord and its two delivery models
ps: A {{neocloud}} owns GPUs and rents time on them. An AI landlord owns the building, the {{substation}}, the cooling plant and the standby power, and rents the hall for years under a {{colocation}} lease while the tenant brings the GPUs. At this company's Ohio site the tenant announced more than US$900 million of its own GPU investment; the landlord spends up to US$1.3 billion on the building and power. Same campus, two balance sheets.

The line between the two can move. 'Turnkey' is 'core/shell construction, MEP installation, operations, and data hall fit-out': a finished hall the tenant racks. 'Turnkey+' adds 'cluster deployment', GPU nodes, InfiniBand or Ethernet networking and storage, so the landlord installs and operates the tenant's compute. Where the line sits decides who signs the equipment orders.

{{Adaptive reuse}}: the campuses are vacant corporate buildings with big feeds, a decommissioned data centre in Ohio and a former retailer's headquarters in Memphis (about 950,000 square feet on 58 acres, bought for US$25 million). Existing structure, existing utility relationship, a shorter path to the first hall than a greenfield.

sections.title: Utility-owned or customer-owned substation
sections.intro: Two ways a campus connects to the grid. The choice decides who buys the largest items in the corpus's equipment list.
rows: Who builds the substation
The utility, at its cost, recovered through a monthly facilities charge
The customer, from a short tap the utility builds off its line
Who buys the high-voltage breakers and step-down {{transformer}}s
The utility
The customer
Where the customer's scope starts
At the {{medium voltage}} {{switchgear}} after the meter
At the transmission tap: substation, transformers, switchgear and everything downstream
Why choose it
Less capital and no lead-time risk for the customer
Speed and control: the utility's queue for building substations is long, and a customer can size its own for later phases
The cost
A monthly charge and the utility's schedule
Two- to four-year {{lead time}}s on large transformers, carried by the customer
This corpus's examples
WhiteFiber's North Carolina campus: the utility owns the 'Extra Facilities (including overhead lines, substations, transformers, breakers, and metering equipment)'
This company's Ohio campus: 'approximately 115-foot-long (0.02 mile) 138-kV transmission line tap … to the new 5C Data Center USA, Inc. substation. The customer will own the Benjamin Substation.'

sections.title: The upfront capacity charge and the two approvals
ps: A municipal utility can charge for a rung of capacity before it exists. Memphis's utility charges data centres an {{upfront capacity charge}} of US$1.52 million per MW: a one-time fee for reserving distribution and transmission capacity, separate from the monthly demand charge. Fifty megawatts costs US$76 million before a kilowatt-hour is used.

Two approvals stand behind it. The municipal utility distributes; the federal power authority behind it generates and transmits. This company's next 50 MW at Memphis 'requires Tennessee Valley Authority approvals' and 'won't advance' before 2027. A landlord can own the building and still not control the date of its power.
The same pattern at the Ohio site: the transmission owner needed a state siting case for a 115-foot tap; the campus's first 25 MW waited on it and on the customer's own substation.

sections.title: Nineteen generators and two kinds of duty
ps: Every large hall carries a fleet of diesel generators that almost never run, sized to the whole load plus redundancy. The city's FAQ for this company's Ohio site counts 3 existing units and 16 more in the first phase; the local press says 19. At roughly 2 to 3 MW each, that is a 75 MW hall's worth of {{standby rating}} machines.

A standby-rated engine runs a few hundred hours a year, mostly in tests, and its {{air permit}} says so: hour limits, ultra-low-sulfur fuel, monthly or fortnightly testing. A {{continuous rating}} engine or a turbine that runs for days is a power plant and needs a plant's permit. The same iron, two very different permits.

This company's Memphis table codes the site 'GRID / BTM' ({{behind-the-meter}}), drone footage showed 'what appeared to be turbines' under construction, and no air permit naming the company or the address was found, in a county whose health department is litigating another operator's turbines. On the public record the generation is unpermitted.

sections.title: What a moratorium is written about
ps: **The pause.** The city passed a six-month {{moratorium}} on data centres above 25 MW (this company exempt); the county limited them to a conditional industrial use with four public meetings; residents petitioned to cap them at 7.5 MW.
**The concerns.** Electric rates, water and generator emissions, in that order in the local record. The servers are not the object; the diesel fleet and the water permit are.

**The consequence.** The next 350 MW at the site will be permitted in that climate. A battery that replaces part of a diesel fleet solves a permitting problem as much as an energy one, which is the pitch a storage seller makes to a landlord facing a moratorium.

sections.title: Direct-to-chip cooling and the water permit
sections.intro: Liquid cooling moves heat with far less air and far less water than the old way, and the water permit is written for the worst day.
rows: {{Cold plate}}s and coolant distribution unit
Carry heat off the GPUs in a rack loop and swap it into the building loop; a 130 kW rack cannot be cooled by air at a sane fan speed
'direct-to-chip liquid cooling'; Phoenix designed to 132 kW per cabinet
{{Closed loop}}
The building loop is sealed and re-used; it consumes no water
'closed loop' with an on-site reservoir planned
{{Dry cooler}}
A radiator with fans that rejects heat to outside air whenever the air is cooler than the coolant
Most of the year
Adiabatic trim
On hot days water is sprayed to cool the air before the dry cooler; the only water the site consumes
'adiabatic trim cooling'; water drawn only above 80°F
Permit against use
The permit is sized for the worst day; use is what the meter shows
300,000 gallons a day permitted; 'around 10% of that' expected
{{PUE}}
Total facility power ÷ IT power; warm-water liquid cooling pushes it toward 1.1–1.3
Not published; the sibling retrofit landlord in this corpus targets 1.3

sections.title: Who signs the order, and for what
ps: **The customer of record.** The landlord's site companies buy the customer-owned substation and its transformers in Ohio, the medium-voltage switchgear, 19 standby generators, {{UPS}}, the cooling loops and the 'prefabricated power skids and cooling modules' its 2026 blogs describe, for each phase it builds. The tenants buy GPUs and networking.
**Scale today.** About 110 MW operational; approved rungs of 25 MW in Ohio and 29 MW in Memphis against announced rungs of 350 and 64 MW.
**What is unnamed.** Every vendor and every EPC. No switchgear, transformer, UPS, generator or cooling supplier appears in any read source.

sections.title: The capital stack of a private landlord
sections.intro: A private company with no published revenue is financed campus by campus. Each layer looks to a different thing for repayment.
rows: Structured equity
Preferred or convertible instruments that behave like debt in bad times and equity in good ones
An infrastructure investor led the equity in a US$835M raise 'through its Infrastructure Structured Solutions strategy'; the borrower was the Ohio campus holding company
Private credit
Loans from funds rather than banks, secured on the campus's leases and the tenant's credit
A bank led the 2025 debt; the same infrastructure investor led US$605M of debt in 2026
Public money
Property-tax abatements and job credits that are part of the return
A 15-year, 100% {{Enterprise Zone}} abatement worth about US$95M in Ohio; a state job credit worth about US$32M to the tenant's parent; a Memphis {{PILOT}} applied for and abandoned
The next round
What it costs to move from operational to roadmap
'an incremental $5 billion or $6 billion in a combination of debt and equity', and an IPO 'absolutely' considered
The arithmetic
At the corpus's US$8–13M per MW, US$1.4B buys 110–175 MW
About what is operational; the next round is the roadmap's price

sections.title: Where an SST, 800 VDC or a battery would enter
ps: Nothing on the company's or its parent's channels mentions {{solid-state transformer}}s, {{800 VDC}} or energy storage; the AMD reference-design work is at rack level. This is an inference from absence.

The customer-owned substation makes the landlord a buyer of conventional step-down transformers and switchgear. A {{solid-state transformer}} would replace the step-down stage inside that scope, so the opening exists in principle at the next campus. A {{BESS}} would enter where the diesel fleet and the moratorium meet.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **Slippage.** 'Operational by early 2026' became 25 MW by September; Memphis 'this summer' (2025) became 20 MW in 2026; the roadmap shrank by a quarter unexplained.
**Unpermitted generation.** Turbine-like construction on a site coded behind-the-meter, with no located air permit, in a county already in court over another operator's turbines.
**A hostile permitting climate.** A moratorium, a county conditional-use rule and a residents' petition at the flagship, and a rejected-in-effect tax freeze at the second site.
**Refinancing dependence.** US$1.4 billion raised against a US$5–6 billion next round; the largest shareholder is also the hardware supplier.

cards.q: What does an AI landlord sell that a neocloud does not?
cards.a: A hall with power, cooling and standby generation under a lease of years; the tenant brings the GPUs. A neocloud owns the GPUs and rents time on them.
The line between landlord and tenant: Turnkey+ adds cluster deployment, so the landlord installs and operates the tenant's compute.

cards.q: Who buys the step-down transformers when 'the customer will own the substation'?
cards.a: The customer, the landlord, along with the high-voltage breakers and the medium-voltage switchgear; the utility supplies the tap.

cards.q: What is an upfront capacity charge?
cards.a: A one-time fee per megawatt for reserving distribution and transmission capacity, paid before any energy is used; separate from the monthly demand charge.

cards.q: Why can a landlord own its building and still not control the date of its power?
cards.a: Because the megawatts arrive in rungs, each gated by a utility or transmission approval, such as a federal power authority's sign-off on the next 50 MW.

cards.q: What is the difference between a standby-rated and a continuous-rated engine?
cards.a: A standby engine runs a few hundred hours a year under an emergency-generator permit; a continuous engine or turbine runs all year and needs a power plant's permit.

cards.q: What are moratoria on data centres usually written about?
cards.a: Electric rates, water and generator emissions: the diesel fleet and the water permit, not the servers.

cards.q: Why is a water permit far larger than water use at a liquid-cooled site?
cards.a: The permit is sized for the hottest day, when adiabatic trim sprays water; the closed loop and dry coolers use none for most of the year.
Preferred or convertible instruments that behave like debt in bad times and like equity in good ones; a way for an infrastructure investor to fund a campus without owning it outright.

cards.q: Where would a solid-state transformer sit at a campus with a customer-owned substation?
cards.a: In the step-down stage inside the customer's own scope, replacing conventional transformers; that is why the opening exists in principle at the next campus.

items.q: A tenant invests US$900 million in a landlord's building. What did the tenant buy?
items.why: The landlord owns the hall, the {{substation}} and the generators, and their equipment orders; the tenant's money is compute.

items.q: A utility filing says 'the customer will own the substation'. Who buys the medium-voltage switchgear?
items.why: With a {{customer-owned substation}} the customer's scope starts at the transmission tap and runs through the {{switchgear}} and everything downstream.

items.q: A utility approves 9 MW and the company's table shows 64 MW next year. What should an equipment vendor size on?
items.why: Equipment is ordered against the approved rung; the 64 MW waits on a federal authority.

items.q: A site has 19 diesel generators under an emergency-use permit. What changes if they run through a summer peak?
c: The permit class: sustained running makes them a power plant
items.why: A {{standby rating}} permit limits hours; continuous running needs a plant's {{air permit}}.

items.q: A permit allows 300,000 gallons a day and the landlord expects to use 30,000. Which figure appears in the moratorium debate?
items.why: The permit is the number opponents quote; the use is what the meter shows. Both are true.

items.q: A landlord has raised US$1.4 billion and states a 1.5 GW roadmap. At US$8–13 million per MW, how much does the money build?
items.why: Roughly what is operational; the stated next round of US$5–6 billion is the roadmap's price.

items.q: Drone footage shows turbines being built at a site coded 'behind-the-meter', and no air permit names the company. What can you conclude?
c: The generation is unpermitted on the public record until a permit names it
items.why: A photograph and a label are not a permit; a construction permit or a plan approval would name the machines.
